newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW - UK Channel 5 set for March 1997 launch.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - UK Channel 5 set for March 1997 launch.

text.p: Britain's fifth terrestrial television channel is now likely to launch in late March 1997, Channel 5 chief executive David Elstein told Reuters on Tuesday.
"What's been widely rumoured in the trade press is an Easter date -- the last weekend of March -- and I wouldn't demur from that," Elstein said in an interview.
Elstein, who joined Channel 5 from BSkyB last month, said he had suggested a specific new date to the Independent Television Commission (ITC), instead of a January 1 debut.
The watchdog will discuss the date on Thursday and Elstein is hopeful it will be possible to confirm it on Friday.

Channel 5 said last month that it would delay its launch for four to six weeks after it was granted access to an additional frequency that would make the new channel available to as many as 1.8 million extra homes.

The new frequency boosted Channel 5's coverage to over 80 percent of the UK but increased the number of homes the company's retuners must visit. The retuners will adjust video recorders to prevent interference from the channel's signal.
Elstein said he had underestimated the number of extra homes which would need retuning when he had originally planned for a delay of a maximum of six weeks.

The granting of the additional frequency meant over three million extra homes would have to be visited by retuners -- those included in the coverage area for the first time plus a sizeable chunk of others now facing potential interference.

Elstein said he believed that Channel 5 would have a maximum of 8,000 retuners working for it. He confirmed that the process would cost around 120 million stg. "It's very unlikely to cost that much less than 120 million. It may cost a little more."
Channel 5 is a consortium comprising UK media groups Pearson and United News & Media plus Luxembourg broadcaster CLT and U.S. investment firm Warburg Pincus.

Elstein said that the three-month delay was insignificant when set against a licence which runs for 10 years. He noted that there was an unexpected financial windfall from the delay as the new channel would not now make its first 22 million stg annual licence payment until January 1998.
"I think the share holders feeling pretty bullish about the whole enterprise," he said. The channel is aiming to break even within three years of its launch.
He said that he hoped to make the channel available via cable and satellite from its start-up. "It means that if people are really interested in Channel 5 they can get it."
Elstein said that the addition of Channel 5 could encourage more viewers to sign up for Sky's satellite package.
"Sky has its own good reasons for wanting to have Channel 5 on satellite. So long as they can find capacity at a price which we can afford we would certainly want to go down that route."
Channel 5's initial programming budget will be only around 110 million stg annually -- considerably smaller than that of its four exisiting terrestrial rivals.

But Elstein said he thought that was a "good, solid sum of money" for Channel 5's plans. "If you commission long runs so that you don't have very high unit costs, if you have a strip schedule where you have the same show every night of the week at the same time and if you concentrate on movies in your nine o'clock peak time slot you're going to get much better value for money," he said.
Most outside estimates are for Channel 5 to take a 5-6 percent share of all viewing and Elstein said that would be a respectable figure to have reached by this time next year.

He said advertisers were fascinated by the prospect of Channel 5, a third national commercial terrestrial network after the mainstream ITV and Channel 4, which has a remit to cater for minority interests.

The new channel was certain to take some advertising business from ITV and Channel 4, said Elstein. But he added that it would also expected advertisers to switch some of their budget away from other media such as print and radio.
-- Keith Weir, London Newsroom +44 171 542 7717
